title: You Are Strong
mood: Team-Up Day, a gap three meters wide around one girl, and one quiet voice from the shade.

hero.alt: A pale blue holographic panel hangs across the front of the Academy's white main building under a clear sky; two cadets in dark uniforms cross the courtyard below it.
hero.credit: Official interactive drama, Guinevere and Vexana

segs.t: A banner hung across the courtyard: THE ASPIRANTS TEAM-UP DAY.
The preparatory course ended today. Aspirants fought in pairs, so this was the day cadets asked each other to be partners. A partner decided how far you went.
Guinevere had planned to be asked before noon. She would say yes graciously.
Her knuckles were still taped, so she had left her gloves off. The tape came from a roll somebody had left on her jacket in the training hall. She had never found out who.
All morning, cadets shook hands around her. Nobody asked.

At noon she gave up waiting. She started toward the boy from her drill line, whose skinned palm she had once patched. He saw her coming and went pink. Before she reached him, he grabbed the hand of the boy beside him.
“Partners!” he said, much too loud.
Guinevere stopped. The crowd had left a gap around her, three meters wide. Nobody stepped into it.
Everyone’s scared of my family’s name,
she thought.
I’ll never find a partner.
On the upper walk at the far side of the courtyard, one other cadet stood alone. It was Layla, the girl with the pink-red twin-tails, her arms on the rail. A boy went up to her with his hand out.
“I’d only have to wait for you,” said Layla. Her voice carried across the courtyard.
He went away again. Guinevere had seen Layla on the field. Nobody kept up with her, and she never slowed down for anyone.
Their eyes met.
She can come over here,
thought Guinevere.
I’m not going over there.
Neither of them moved. After a while Layla turned back to the rail, and Guinevere found the fountain very interesting.
It stood against the courtyard wall, under the brass plaque of the patrons. HOUSE BAROQUE came first. Two cadets were filling their flasks beneath it.
“Her score was bought,” said one.
“Of course,” said the other. “Her father’s name did the fighting.”
They had not lowered their voices much.
Guinevere’s chin went up. It took effort.
Her hand went to her breast pocket. The paper had been in it for days, folded along its soft fold.
Top score,
in red ink, beside three sets of initials.
Nobody bought those,
she thought.
And he didn’t even come out of his office.
She turned her back on the fountain, so they would not see her face.
“You are strong, Guinevere.”

The voice came from the shade of the side wall, six strides off. A black-haired girl stood there alone with her arms folded. It was Vexana, from the shelter bench. In a whole year Guinevere had heard her say maybe ten words.
She had not raised her voice. Behind Guinevere, the whisperers stopped. Only the fountain kept running.
Guinevere did not say anything. For once she could not.
Her hand came away from her pocket.
She said my name,
she thought.
Everyone else says Baroque. He never says it at all.
Vexana did not look away. Her violet eyes had a hard light far back in them. Guinevere knew that look. She saw it in her own mirror every morning, when she tied her bows.
Behind her, the two at the fountain capped their flasks and found somewhere else to be.
Guinevere crossed the gap in six strides. She held out her bare, taped hand.
“Be my partner!”
Vexana’s eyes went to the hand and stayed there.
“No.”
She walked off along the wall with her arms still folded. Over her shoulder she said, “You’re strong. You need a strong partner.”
Guinevere stood with her hand out to nobody. She took it back.
No one had ever turned down the great lady Guinevere before!
She waited to mind. She found she did not mind one bit.
She said no to me,
she thought.
Not to the name. To me.
She watched the black hair go in under the arch.
Vexana kept her arms folded until she was through the arch. In the empty corridor beyond it, she let them drop.
I said her name,
she thought. She had never said it aloud before. She had not meant to say anything at all.
But
bought

was a lie. Vexana had run the same trial and seen who won it. She had seen the girl come back the next night, late, with bare hands, and hit the bag until there was blood on it. Whatever that was, nobody had bought it.
I only said what was true,
she thought.
I never said I’d stand beside her.
The hand held out to her had been wound in cloth tape, the kind she wound on her staff’s grip. Her own roll, from the jacket on the bench. Guinevere had used it.
A partner stood at your back. When a claw came down, a partner stepped in front of it.
Her father had done that once. All she had seen was his back in his Shield coat, between her and a raised claw. She had watched it over a soldier’s shoulder. He had stayed.
She’d do the same,
thought Vexana.
She never stops for anything. She wouldn’t stop for a claw.
Nobody was going to die for her again. And she would not stand where she might have to watch it.
You need a strong partner.
She had meant someone else, someone who would never need saving. Not Vexana. She had run out of the shelter by the wall.

She had watched Guinevere every night for a year. On the night after the trial, she had taken one step down the gallery stair toward the lamp, and stopped. When she did go down, it was only as far as the bench by the door.
I like her,
she thought.
That’s why it has to be no.
At the gate, on the first morning, she had thought,
Like a lamp.
Behind her now, through the arch, the courtyard lay bright in the noon sun. She kept her back to it.
She’s all light. I’d only bring her the dark.
Her hand had started to shake. She closed it in her pocket, around the new roll of tape, and walked on.
The next day.
Guinevere waited at the top of the main stairs. Every cadet came down them sooner or later. She had a speech ready. It had four points.
Vexana came along the landing with a book under her arm.
“Vexana. Be my partner. First...”
“No.”
All four points went out of Guinevere’s head. She went down two steps after her.
“You said I’m strong. How would you know?”
Vexana stopped. “I have seen you in the training hall at night. Bare fists first. Then the drones.”
“You watched me?!”
“Yes.”
Guinevere’s face went hot.
Every night?
she thought.
Even that one?
She put her hands on her hips. “Then why not? Give me one reason.”
Vexana looked past her, at the window on the landing.
“Feelings are illusions forbidden by the night.”
“What does that even mean?”
“It means no.”
Vexana went on down the stairs. She did not hurry.
Guinevere stayed where she was.
Feelings,
she thought.
She said feelings.
“That’s two,” she told the empty stairs.
She was grinning, and she could not stop.
